implementation_notes: A scala.concurrent.Future is created by Future.apply and memoises its outcome, so one future may be observed by any number of callers and awaiting it repeatedly yields the same value or the same failure; the registry is a concurrent map (java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap, TrieMap, or computeIfAbsent) from key to Future, with removal in an onComplete callback. The ExecutionContext supplies the thread that runs the computation, so creating the Future inside the map's compute step must not block that step. cats-effect's Deferred/memoize and zio-cache provide the effect-typed equivalents with the same semantics - one execution no matter how many callers - when the codebase is effect-based rather than Future-based.
pitfalls: A Future cannot be cancelled: a caller that gives up abandons its own wait (Await.result timeout, a race) while the computation runs to completion for the others.
Failure is memoised and shared: every waiter sees the same Throwable, and a failed entry left in the registry blocks all later callers - remove unconditionally on completion.
computeIfAbsent's mapping function must not call back into the same map for the same key: a recursive load for that key deadlocks or throws.
Blocking inside the ExecutionContext (Await.result inside a Future body, or heavy work on the global EC) can starve the pool; keep flight bodies non-blocking or give them a dedicated EC.
A Future captures its ExecutionContext at creation, so the flight runs on the starter's pool - a per-request EC that shuts down would strand the other waiters.
